items.title: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen! - TechCrunch
items.summary: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!  TechCrunch
items.content:
The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims.
The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China's intelligence service.
While Jensen Huang's relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia's potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang.
U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country's leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff.
Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot's Kimi's K3 releases and DeepSeek's V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips.
White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination.
That doesn't mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch's data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025.
However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed.
"If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn't make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want," Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer.
Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai.
In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a " China problem " because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed's relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang's companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips.
Ironically, short-seller Culper's bet against Nvidia wasn't driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government's response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry.
If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven't been cleared for import.
Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn't buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips.
For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang's personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed's data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate.
The U.S. government's treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials.

items.content:
Howard Lutnick's sons' Nvidia ties amid Jensen Huang China spy scandal
Cantor Fitzgerald’s reported Nvidia share count fell by nearly half between September 2025 and March 2026, a CNBC analysis found.
That was the period when, according to Axios, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced pressure from administration officials to address suspected smuggling of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China.
The Wall Street firm, which Lutnick formerly chaired and is now run by his sons, maintained extensive commercial ties to Nvidia, helping arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies in its AI business universe and repeatedly hosting its top executives.
Those relationships have come into sharper focus following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and revelations about Lutnick’s handling of national security concerns involving the chipmaker. There is no evidence that Cantor's business interests influenced Lutnick's decisions.
Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick looks on as President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., June 11, 2026.
In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC.
"We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock.
Yet the firm, formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026 , according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings.
The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, Axios reported Nov. 11.
By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to a Nov. 10 Axios report, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina.
Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership.
Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5.
An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia.
Richard Painter , the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota, said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great."
"His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC.
There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions.
"Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC.
Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick, Brandon Lutnick and Kyle Lutnick did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings.
As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday.
Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary.
But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."
Bessent pointed to Commerce as the department responsible for imposing the entity list, which identifies restricted businesses and other groups, adding, "You will have to ask them about their internal processes."
CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang (L) and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick listen during an announcement to renovate Washington Dulles International Airport, in the Oval Office of the White House on July 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
Nvidia was Cantor's second-largest reported stock position before Howard Lutnick left Wall Street to become commerce secretary in February 2025, behind only bitcoin investor MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy . At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth $479 million, according to its quarterly securities filing .
That share count held steady through September 2025, but its value climbed 36% to $652 million, according to Cantor's quarterly securities filing , as the Trump administration moved over the summer to ease restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China .
Over the following six months, however, the number of Nvidia shares Cantor reported holding fell by 49%, to 3 million in December and 1.78 million by the end of March 2026 , with their value dropping from $652 million to $310 million, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings.
Pressure on Howard Lutnick was also mounting on Capitol Hill. Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., in March urged the secretary to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after three people linked to Nvidia customer Super Micro Computer were indicted on charges of conspiring to smuggle AI chips to China.
"The Trump administration, I think, leaks like a sieve when it comes to nonpublic government information getting to various hedge fund guys," Painter said, though he stressed there is no evidence Howard Lutnick had shared such information with his sons.
The filings do not establish why Cantor's reported share count fell or whether its overall financial exposure to Nvidia declined. Nvidia’s stock had more than doubled from its April 2025 lows by late October, before retreating in the following months. The stock fell about 6.5% between the end of September and the end of March.
Cantor's reported Nvidia holdings remained near that lower level through June 30 , the latest quarter covered by public disclosures, at 1.81 million shares. Its next quarterly filing is due Monday.
Most of those shares were attributed to CF Secured , a Cantor brokerage subsidiary that uses stocks and derivatives to hedge customer transactions, according to its audited financial statements. Cantor also disclosed substantial Nvidia options positions during the time period CNBC examined, overwhelmingly skewed toward put options, which can protect against declines in the stock price.
As concerns about Huang escalated inside the Trump administration in May, according to the Nov. 11 Axios report, Cantor was helping finance the expansion of one of Nvidia's newest business partners, securities filings show .
On May 7, Nvidia and Australia-based cloud computing provider IREN announced a five-year, $3.4 billion cloud computing contract and a strategic partnership giving the chipmaker the right to invest up to $2.1 billion in IREN.
"That's not a passive financial investment. Nvidia is a partner who wins as we deliver," IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told investors on the company's quarterly earnings call that day.
Five days later, as Trump headed to China aboard Air Force One, Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned him about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, The New York Times reported Tuesday. Huang, who had not initially been invited on the trip, joined the president's delegation during a refueling stop in Alaska.
Howard Lutnick had already been sent a highly classified intelligence memo detailing concerns about Huang's relationship, according to the Nov. 10 Axios report.
On May 12, the day Trump departed for China, IREN announced the pricing of a convertible bond offering that ultimately raised $3 billion when it closed two days later. Cantor was one of seven bookrunners on the deal, alongside JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs .
On the day the offering closed, May 14, Lutnick's Commerce Department quietly cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies , including Alibaba and ByteDance, to buy Nvidia's advanced H200 chips, though some of those approvals predated the intelligence memo.
It is unclear when IREN hired Cantor for the offering or how much the firm earned from the deal. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.
Cantor reported a substantial position in IREN's stock.
By the end of June, Cantor reported $115 million in IREN shares and $362 million in Nvidia shares. Together, the two companies accounted for more than 9% of the value of Cantor's reported $5.2 billion in securities holdings, excluding options, according to CNBC's analysis of the filing.
Brandon Lutnick, chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald, speaks during the Bitcoin 2025 conference in Las Vegas, Nevada, on May 29, 2025.
IREN was not the only company in Nvidia's orbit that turned to Cantor for financing.
In October 2025, Cantor advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal to support its data center campus in Abilene, Texas, the first site of Stargate, the massive AI infrastructure project backed by OpenAI , SoftBank and Oracle .
Newmark, a commercial real estate firm controlled by Cantor , also helped finance the Abilene campus, arranging a $7.1 billion construction loan in May 2025.
Ten months later, Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion for a roughly 20% stake in Lancium, with up to $1 billion more tied to future milestones, The Information reported in August. Lancium , which is also backed by Blackstone, confirmed an investment and a technology partnership on Aug. 24 without disclosing financial terms.
It's unclear whether Cantor continued advising Lancium after the financing deal or played a role in Nvidia's investment. Neither Cantor nor Lancium responded to questions about the investment.
Cantor's reported ties also extend to Nvidia's supply chain.
In May 2025, days after Howard Lutnick announced the transfer of his ownership stake in Cantor to his children via trusts, Semafor reported that bankers at the firm had informally advised executives at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. , which makes Nvidia's most advanced chips, on navigating Washington. Cantor called Semafor's report "baseless and false."
TSMC received billions of dollars in federal subsidies created during the Biden administration and administered by the Commerce Department to fund its U.S. manufacturing expansion.
Democratic senators called for an ethics investigation in December into whether the Lutnick family stood to benefit from Howard Lutnick's push to expand AI data centers.
And on Wednesday, Sens. Warren and Chris Coons , D-Del., demanded that Howard Lutnick, Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve records on Nvidia's chip exports to China and intelligence warnings about Huang.
The senators questioned whether "prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken or national security recommendations were overruled."
"The place where I think the Trump administration has most failed here is in being persuaded by Jensen Huang and others to license the export of some advanced chips," Coons said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box," accusing the administration of turning a blind eye to the black market for more advanced chips.

Former Hamas bodyguard convicted of Birmingham knife crime also wanted in Germany
Mohammed Alfatih rearrested over alleged plot to target Israelis in Europe while detained for attack on bailiff
A former Hamas bodyguard convicted of knife crime in the UK is wanted in Germany for allegedly plotting to murder Jewish people.
Details of the alleged plot can now be reported after Mohammed Alfatih, also known as Mohammed Naim, was found guilty on Friday of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his home in Birmingham .
The 40-year-old was found guilty by a majority verdict of unlawful wounding, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of the more serious charge of wounding with intent.
He was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit when he attacked the bailiff last year.
Alfatih, the son of a senior Hamas official, could not be named during his trial because of reporting restrictions.
He had been photographed working for a former leader of Hamas before being granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.
While detained for the attack on the bailiff in Birmingham, he was rearrested after authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged plot to attack Israeli targets in central Europe .
Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK, with his connection to Hamas stated in the German extradition request.
German prosecutors charged seven suspected Hamas members in September over an alleged plot to target Jews or Israelis in Germany or Austria around the second anniversary of the 7 October attack on Israel.
They said “Mohammed A” played a prominent role in transporting and storing weapons but was being prosecuted separately after UK authorities arrested him in London and noted he had not yet been returned to Germany.
German authorities said he was connected to Hamas’s leadership and was said to have produced a video in advance to take responsibility for the attack on its behalf.
The attack was disrupted by Germany’s domestic intelligence service after a tipoff from the Mossad, Israel’s secret service.
During a two-week trial at Birmingham crown court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October 2025.
The bailiff, Kevin Bucknall, was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment. The defendant pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.
The jurors, who convicted Alfatih after being shown footage of him brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in Kings Heath, Birmingham, were not told of his links to Hamas.
They were also not told Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit after being released on bail on suspicion of a terror offence days before the bailiff was attacked.
A government source said: “This is a staggering example of the loss of border control under the last Conservative government, who granted his asylum claim and gave him citizenship.
“This Labour government has just introduced reforms that ensure those who gain citizenship must first show they are a good citizen and have contributed to this country.”

items.title: Goldman Sachs sees a new problem emerging for the Federal Reserve - Yahoo Finance
items.summary: Goldman Sachs sees a new problem emerging for the Federal Reserve  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
Goldman Sachs sees a new problem emerging for the Federal Reserve
It took one inflation report to make one of Wall Street's most closely watched forecasters change its mind. Goldman Sachs no longer believes December's rate hike will close out the Fed's tightening cycle, and the bank now has company in rewriting its outlook.
Analysts across Wall Street reacted quickly after a third straight month of bad inflation news, with some now openly questioning the Fed's recent choices. The debate is no longer about whether rates rise next month, but how far the Fed will have to go after that.
Goldman's timing rests on a specific view of how prices will behave over the winter. Chief U.S. economist David Mericle expects inflation to cool through the end of the year before fresh price pressures at the start of 2027 push it higher again, which is why he favors March over January for the next move, Reuters reported.
Also read: Goldman Sachs has a new warning for the housing market for 2027
What worried Mericle most was how broad the increases were. He said that the October report showed upside surprises across several categories that the energy shock from the Iran war cannot fully explain. He still sees inflation meaningfully lower by the end of 2027, but only if the Fed takes a tougher line first.
The numbers behind that call were hard to ignore. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, ahead of the 0.3% economists expected, while core prices climbed 0.3% against a forecast of 0.2%, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics . Food, rent and medical care all moved higher during the month.
Goldman's list of culprits closely aligns with Vanguard's. Vanguard senior U.S. economist Josh Hirt traced the pressure to tariffs, energy prices and demand tied to the AI buildout, and the firm expected one more hike before the end of 2026, with the Fed holding steady in 2027.
Bank of America is leaning closer to Deutsche Bank's timetable than to Goldman's. Its analysts kept their call for a quarter-point move in December, but warned that the Fed is falling behind on inflation and flagged a rising risk that the next hike comes in January rather than March. They also said the October hold is starting to look like a policy mistake.
A bigger December move is also getting a closer look. BofA Global Research, Citi and Standard Chartered said recent data and Waller's comments have opened the door to a half-point hike, though they noted the evidence is not yet strong enough to firmly back it, as reported by Reuters. Standard Chartered economists led by Steve Englander said the case is stronger than they had expected, but still not definitive.
PGIM had already gone further than most. Its midyear outlook called for precautionary hikes against inflation shocks, and by the end of October, its team saw at least two more quarter-point increases ahead.
Not everyone was on that page before the data hit. J.P. Morgan expected just one more hike, most likely in December. Chief U.S. economist Michael Feroli argued that inflation still appeared to be driven by supply shocks, as reported by J.P. Morgan. Goldman held a similar end-of-cycle view until this week, underscoring how quickly the October numbers changed the conversation.
Goldman Sachs no longer believes December's rate hike will close out the Fed's tightening cycle.Nexpher Images / Getty Images Fed hawks are backing up Goldman's new call
Waller set the tone just hours before the data landed. He said the Fed should consider a half-point move in December if inflation came in hot, and that going smaller would risk its credibility. October's report then landed above forecasts, and suddenly his warning had more weight.
Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan went a step further. She said the committee needs at least two more quarter-point increases and that it is unacceptable for inflation not to be heading back to the Fed's 2% target. That path lines up neatly with the December and March hikes Goldman now expects.
Scott Bessent just reframed the case for a December rate hike
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh reveals October surprise inside interest-rate pause
How a Fed interest rate pause would impact Main Street investors
The AI boom is part of that discussion too. Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin said the surge in AI infrastructure spending is adding to near-term inflation by fueling strong demand, while Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee urged officials to confront the risk of overheating, TheStreet reported. AI-related investment was one of the inflation drivers Goldman highlighted as well.
Bond traders reacted quickly. The two-year Treasury yield, which closely tracks expectations for Fed policy, jumped sharply after the release. Higher long-term yields feed directly into mortgage and car loan rates.
The next test for Goldman's call comes before the Fed meets on December 8 and December 9. October's CPI was the last consumer price report policymakers will see before then, though they will still get the personal consumption expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, later this month.
For households, Goldman's pushback on its rate-cut timeline means cheaper borrowing isn't arriving anytime soon. The October numbers offered little comfort to anyone already stretched by high prices. A longer tightening cycle keeps loan rates up well into next year.
Credit card rates tend to move closely with the Fed, so each additional hike increases the cost of carrying a balance. Savers sit on the other side of that trade, earning more on high-yield accounts and CDs for as long as rates stay up.

items.content:
Wall Street extended its losses on Friday, November 13, as mounting uncertainty surrounding Nvidia ( NVDA -2.01% ) and rising Treasury yields fueled a sharp sell-off in technology stocks. As of 11:31 a.m. ET, the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.91% ) led major indexes lower, falling 1.45% to 24,998, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.40% ) declined 0.82% to 7,530. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.10% ) proved more resilient, slipping just 0.12% to 52,234 as investors rotated away from high-growth technology companies.
Meanwhile, the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.10%, adding pressure to equity valuations following another round of inflation data. Gold edged 0.13% lower to $3,880.40, while defensive consumer stocks outperformed. Technology and real estate shares suffered some of the steepest losses, highlighting growing concerns about elevated borrowing costs and the outlook for economic growth.
Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD -8.75% ) plunged 9.89% as selling pressure intensified across the semiconductor industry following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Cisco Systems ( CSCO -6.24% ) also declined 5.70%, reflecting broader weakness in enterprise technology stocks.
Elsewhere, Modine Manufacturing ( MOD +27.86% ) surged 28.41% following reports that Samsung Electronics ( SSNLF +0.00% ) was exploring a potential acquisition of the thermal management company. Nu Holdings ( NU +11.75% ) also bucked the broader market decline, climbing 10.95% as investors favored select financial technology stocks.
Friday's sell-off underscores the growing vulnerability of the AI trade to both company-specific uncertainty and tighter financial conditions. Nvidia's leadership transition has raised questions about the future of the industry's dominant chipmaker, while renewed selling in AMD and other semiconductor stocks suggests concerns are spreading across the broader AI supply chain. With Nvidia scheduled to report earnings next week, investors will be looking for reassurance that demand, product development, and customer spending remain intact despite the leadership shakeup.
Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield's climb above 5% presents a significant challenge for equity valuations. Higher yields increase the attractiveness of fixed-income investments and raise the cost of financing future growth, particularly for capital-intensive technology companies. Although the rotation toward defensive sectors suggests investors are becoming more cautious, a sustained market recovery will likely depend on stabilizing yields, resilient corporate earnings, and greater clarity surrounding Federal Reserve policy.

UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
Eurotunnel owner Getlink wants to replicate ‘airport experience’ at Folkestone and Calais, without making people get out of cars
Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais .
In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France.
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further.
Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais.
New airport style drive-in biometrics kiosks at Eurotunnel in Calais. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate.
In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore.
The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years.
EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France , have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues.
The new drive-in fingerprinting terminals at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal.
Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting.
But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting.
Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time.
“This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?”
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said.
The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent.
Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche.
He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars.
The new drive-in border controls at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint.
Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they are can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question was are asking all the time.”
This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

For more than a decade, Fatih Birol has been one of the world’s most influential voices in energy markets. As the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA), he advises presidents and energy ministers; CEOs follow his view of the market with careful attention.
When we caught up at the United Nations climate change conference, known as COP31 , currently underway in Antalya, Turkey, he offered a blunt analysis: the war in Iran has unleashed a structural shift. "I don't see any credible pathway in which the world of energy is going back where it was before the Iran War," he said on Nov. 13.
A quick analysis might boil this shift down to simple terms. In general, the focus on energy security will mean more renewable energy because it can be produced locally. It will mean efficiency measures so that countries use less fuel and are less vulnerable to shocks. Indeed, an energy crisis policy tracker from the IEA cites dozens of policies countries have laid out this year to do just that—from a push for biodiesel in Indonesia to incentives for consumers to install solar and storage in Bangladesh.
By signing up you are agreeing to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy .
But Birol says the coming structural changes in energy will have even wider implications, shaping economic and geopolitical outcomes. He cites economic diversification plans from oil-exporting countries, new trade partnerships, and investments in new technologies like next-generation batteries and nuclear power. All of which comes with an eye toward safeguarding energy supply from supply disruptions. "Instead of importing energy, they are deciding to build energy,” he told me.
A key theme in Antalya—and on Birol’s mind—is electrification. Right now less than a quarter of final energy consumption comes from electricity. The rest comes primarily from fuel consumption, think of petrol in vehicles, heating oil in homes, or gas in stoves. Relying on electricity, which tends to be produced relatively close to where it’s used, addresses energy security concerns. That’s even more the case when electricity is produced using renewables rather than imported fossil fuels.
The COP31 presidency is pushing countries to pledge to rely on electricity for 35% of their final energy consumption by 2035. The world’s electricity grid still relies on fossil fuels to some degree—more or less so depending on the area—but today it’s typically cleaner than most fossil fuels. It will be even cleaner as renewable deployment continues.
Electrification also represents a structural shift. It promises to reshape trade relationships as countries need to either build clean technology supply chains or identify friendly partners to build relevant trade relationships. It will spur investment in the power sector, advancing both big electric infrastructure projects and creating new companies that build innovative electricity technologies. In the IEA’s special report on electrification released in September, the agency says that annual global investment in electricity generation, battery storage, and grids could total $2.5 trillion by 2035 in a scenario where electrification really takes off. That’s a $1 trillion increase from last year. And electrification promises to unlock—or at least lessen—the stranglehold that oil and gas has on geopolitics while elevating the importance of another set of resources, including critical minerals.
“Two years ago, I said we are entering the age of electricity,” Birol told me. “I can tell you today, when I look at today's numbers, we are in the age of electricity."

Ukrainian soldiers run toward their positions through a ‘kill zone’ exposed to Russian drone attacks in the Druzhkivka area of eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region. Photograph: Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images
Ukrainian soldiers run toward their positions through a ‘kill zone’ exposed to Russian drone attacks in the Druzhkivka area of eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region. Photograph: Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images
Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Starshield restrictions continue on ‘entire front line’
Curbs on SpaceX system are making it hard to intercept drones and sending a bad signal to Russia, says Ukrainian president. What we know on day 1,725
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said ⁠speed restrictions remain in place on the US Starshield satellite communications system , hampering ⁠the Ukrainian military’s ability ⁠to ​operate inside the country. The continued restrictions made it hard to intercept jet-powered and other ⁠drones and sent a bad signal to Russia on dealing with land seized by Russian forces ⁠in the war, the Ukrainian president also said on Friday. “Unfortunately, the speed restrictions remain in place ​along the entire front line ‌and in temporarily-occupied ‌territories of Ukraine,” he said in his nightly video address. “I expect ‌the ministry of defence and the foreign ministry, together with all relevant structures in the United States, will work through this issue.” Ukrainian officials said in mid-October that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had abruptly capped the speed of Starlink and its Starshield military version amid tensions with ​the US over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Service was restored on 24 October.
Zelenskyy said on Thursday Ukrainian military units had recorded ​disruptions to ​Starshield over several days. He repeated that the restrictions “limit our ​ability to ‌intercept jet-powered ​Shaheds [Iranian-designed drones] ​and counter other drones”. “They also send Russia a signal that America may somehow treat our temporarily-occupied land differently,” he said. “We expect the speed to be restored.”
Russia attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassies , after Zelenskyy’s comments on the throttling of Starshield . Three people were injured when a drone smashed into the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics at 3am, hitting the second floor of the hospital and an adjoining 19th-century building in the capital, reports Luke Harding . Meanwhile, Russia claimed to have shot down nearly 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, one of the largest swarms sent by Kyiv. It said at least four people were killed in the southern region of Volgograd.
The EU’s foreign policy chief warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression, reports Jennifer Rankin . “We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021.
Russia has been rocked by two car bomb attacks that killed a senior military figure and seriously injured a suspected intelligence agent, in the latest in a series of assassination attempts believed to have been orchestrated by Kyiv. On Friday morning a car bomb exploded in southern Moscow, severely injuring Sergei Zavorotniy, 72, a former senior aide to Ukraine’s exiled former prime minister Mykola Azarov, reports Pjotr Sauer . The blast came a day after a car bomb explosion in St Petersburg killed a senior Russian military official. The official has not been publicly identified but a local broadcaster cited sources as saying the victim was a colonel in the Russian air force.
Russian forces launched strikes on two ⁠Ukrainian cities on Friday , killing one person ⁠and injuring more than ⁠50 ​in the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia and killing ⁠two more in the Black Sea port of ⁠Odesa, regional officials said. In Zaporizhzhia, a ​five-storey apartment ‌building was ‌hit and seriously damaged. A rescue worker was killed when a concrete slab collapsed during operations to clear rubble, regional governor ‌Mykhailo Semikin said. In Odesa, two people died in an ⁠attack on a private residence, ​said the city’s military administration hed, Serhiy Lysak. Five people ​were ​injured.
A general in Ukraine’s SBU security service suspected in a serious corruption case was released from pre-trial detention on Friday after posting $1.2m bail. Footage on Ukraine’s TSN.ua news site showed Serhiy Duka after leaving prison proclaiming his innocence and thanking his SBU “brothers-in-arms” who had raised the bail money. Duka was detained on 4 November as part of an anti-corruption operation targeting an alleged criminal group that investigators say involved members of the SBU, the prosecutor’s office, the police and organised crime.
